entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Louis de Bourbon-Vendôme (died March 23, 1557), a cardinal and Bishop of Laon, stood as a prominent French *prince du sang* and ecclesiastical statesman during the tumultuous early decades of the French Renaissance. As the second son of Francis, Count of Vendôme, and Marie of Luxembourg, he embodied the complex interplay of aristocratic lineage, political ambition, and spiritual authority characteristic of 16th-century France. His career spanned the reigns of Francis I and Henry II, placing him at the heart of royal councils, diplomatic missions, and the Gallican Church's efforts to maintain its autonomy against both papal and burgeoning Protestant pressures. He was instrumental in shaping religious policy and exercising significant influence over the French court's domestic and foreign affairs.

Elevated to the cardinalate by Pope Clement VII in 1534, Louis de Bourbon-Vendôme's ecclesiastical career was marked by a rapid accumulation of benefices, including the bishoprics of Laon (1510), Luçon (1524), and Saintes (1524), along with several rich abbeys. He served as Abbot of Saint-Denis from 1515, a position of considerable prestige and wealth. Beyond his spiritual roles, he engaged actively in diplomacy, participating in the negotiations of the Treaty of Crépy (1544) between Francis I and Emperor Charles V, which temporarily halted the Italian Wars. His consistent support for the French monarchy, particularly in its struggle against Habsburg dominance and its management of internal religious dissent, solidified his position as a trusted royal advisor.

entities.summary:
Louis de Bourbon, Prince du Sang and Cardinal of Vendôme (1493–1557), served as a pivotal ecclesiastical and political figure in 16th-century France during the reigns of Francis I and Henry II. Born at Château de Ham, he was the second son of Francis, Count of Vendôme, and Marie of Luxembourg, placing him at the nexus of the French royal family and the high nobility. His career spanned the turbulent period of the Italian Wars and the nascent stages of the Reformation, where he leveraged his princely status and extensive ecclesiastical appointments to influence both church policy and dynastic affairs, particularly through his role as Archbishop of Sens and later as Papal Legate.

Elevated to the cardinalate by Pope Leo X in 1517 at the age of 24, Louis de Bourbon accumulated a significant portfolio of benefices, including the Archbishopric of Sens (1525–1557) and the Bishoprics of Laon (1510–1552) and Luçon (1514–1524). Beyond his spiritual duties, he acted as a trusted royal advisor and diplomat, notably participating in the negotiations for the Treaty of Madrid in 1526, which aimed to secure the release of King Francis I from Habsburg captivity. His consistent presence in the French royal council underscored his influence in shaping foreign policy and mediating domestic political struggles, including those between the powerful Guise and Montmorency factions.
